script: My grandmother wrote every recipe wrong on purpose, and we did not find out until we spread all thirty one cards on her kitchen table, the week after we buried her. But the mistakes were not random. Every single card was wrong in a different place. Mine said two teaspoons of salt. My cousin's said forty minutes instead of twenty. My mother's left out the eggs completely. For years we thought she was slipping. My mother used to call her from the kitchen, phone against her shoulder, flour on her hands. Ma, it says two teaspoons. That cannot be right. And my grandmother would say, oh, let me think. And she would take her time. And she would give her the real amount, and then she would ask how the children were, and they would talk for forty minutes. That happened every Sunday for eleven years. At the table, my aunt counted the errors on each card. She did it out loud, like a woman checking a bill she already knows is wrong. Three on this one. Five on this one. Mine had seven. I said the number like a confession. Seven. I thought it meant she trusted me least, that she thought I could not follow a simple list. My aunt did not look up. She said, no. She gave the most mistakes to the ones she most wanted to hear from. We went through all thirty one. And near the bottom of the pile there was one card with no mistakes at all. Not one. Every measurement exactly right, written out clean, in a hand steadier than the others because it was written years earlier. It belonged to my aunt Elena. Elena had not spoken to her in nine years. Nobody at that table said anything for a long time. My mother put the card back down very carefully, the way you put down something that belongs to someone else. Elena got the recipe. The rest of us got the phone calls. She never told any of us. Not one of us, not once, in fifty one years.

Thirty one cards. Every one of them wrong in a different place. My aunt counted the errors out loud and mine had seven, and I thought I knew what that meant.

One card had no mistakes at all.

Who called you every Sunday?
